explanation: Brisk means lively and rapid, so "quick" is the synonym. "breeze" is merely something often called brisk, not a definition of it. "sluggish" reverses the meaning. A brisk manner is short rather than "polite", and speed is the point, so "thorough" misses it.

To conceal is to keep from being seen, that is, to "hide". "reveal" and "discover" both mean bringing to light, the reverse. "shelter" is what hiding sometimes provides but is not the same act, and "console" merely looks and sounds similar.

Deft describes neat, expert handling, so "skillful" is correct. "clumsy" is its opposite. "swift" tempts because deft movements are often fast, but speed without skill is not deftness. "silent" borrows from a similar looking word about hearing, and "stubborn" is unrelated.

To curb an impulse is to hold it back, so "restrain" fits. "sidewalk" belongs to the other, street-edge sense but names a neighboring thing rather than defining the word. "encourage" is the opposite, "punish" is a different response to bad behavior, and "surround" confuses enclosing with limiting.

To bolster an argument is to prop it up, so "support" is the synonym. "weaken" is the opposite. "mattress" points to the long pillow that shares the name but does not define the verb. "boast" is a sound-alike about bragging, and "decorate" adds ornament rather than strength.

To divulge a secret is to make it known, so "reveal" is correct. "conceal" is the opposite. "indulge" looks and sounds close but means giving in to a desire. "whisper" names a manner of speaking, not disclosure, and "exaggerate" distorts information rather than releasing it.

In its verb sense, to brook no argument is to put up with none, so "tolerate" is correct. "trout" belongs to the small-stream sense as a thing found there, not a definition. "forbid" is the opposite, "ignore" is refusing to notice rather than allowing, and "wander" borrows from the idea of water winding along.

Desultory effort jumps from one thing to another without a plan, so "aimless" fits. "methodical" is its opposite. "gloomy" is pulled in by the similar looking word for barren and deserted, and "rude" by the word for an offensive remark. "exhausting" describes strain, which desultory work usually avoids.

A dearth of rain is a shortage of it, so "scarcity" is the synonym. "abundance" is the opposite. "sorrow" is drawn in by a grim sounding relative of the word, "depth" merely resembles it in spelling, and "expense" names a common consequence of a shortage rather than the shortage itself.

To "grumble" is to voice discontent in a low, muttering way, so "complain" is the match. "Stumble" only resembles the stem in sound and means to trip. "Whisper" captures the low volume of grumbling but not the discontent, and a whisper may be perfectly cheerful. "Boast" and "congratulate" both express approval rather than dissatisfaction, so neither can substitute.

"Feeble" describes a lack of strength, which is exactly what "weak" means. "Sturdy" is its opposite. "Fickle" merely looks and sounds similar; it means changeable in loyalty or preference. "Gentle" describes mildness of manner, which a very strong person can show, and "hollow" describes an empty interior, which is a matter of structure rather than of strength.

To "imitate" is to copy the manner or appearance of something, which is what "mimic" means. "Irritate" is the near look-alike and means to annoy. "Admire" names a common motive for copying someone but not the act of copying. "Ridicule" is what mockery adds to imitation; imitation by itself need not mock. "Invent" is the opposite activity, producing something with no model to follow.

To "exacerbate" a problem is to make it more severe, so "worsen" is the synonym. "Soothe" is the opposite. "Infuriate" belongs to the frequently confused word "exasperate" and applies to people rather than to conditions. "Excavate" merely shares the opening sound and means to dig out. "Postpone" delays a difficulty instead of intensifying it.

A "furtive" glance is one taken secretly, so as not to be noticed; "stealthy" carries that same sense of concealed movement. "Aboveboard" means open and honest and is the opposite. "Festive" is the look-alike trap. "Hurried" is tempting because secret acts are often quick, but speed is not secrecy. "Thrifty" describes careful spending, a different kind of care entirely.

To "linger" is to stay on longer than expected, moving away slowly if at all, which is what "dawdle" describes. "Hasten" and "depart" both remove the person from the scene and so reverse the idea. "Mingle" resembles the stem in sound and means to circulate among a group, something one can do briskly. "Sulk" names a mood rather than a way of remaining.

"Lofty" describes something of great height, so "towering" matches it. "Lowly" is the opposite. "Attic" is drawn from the related word "loft" and names a place rather than a quality. "Spacious" concerns room in every direction, and a wide hall can be spacious without being high. "Drafty" describes a cold current of air that a tall room may happen to have.

To "humor" someone is to go along with a whim in order to keep the peace, which is what "indulge" means. "Joke" belongs to the comic sense of the word but names a thing one tells rather than an action of yielding. "Thwart" and "criticize" both oppose the person instead of accommodating them. "Moisten" plays on the old use of the word for bodily fluids and fits no current meaning.

"Laconic" describes speech that uses very few words, so "terse" is the synonym. "Long-winded" is its opposite. "Lackadaisical" is the look-alike and means listless. "Relaxed" borrows from "lax" and describes ease of manner rather than economy of speech. "Sarcastic" is tempting because brief remarks are often cutting, but a laconic reply can be perfectly sincere.

To "mend" something is to fix what is broken or torn, which is exactly what "repair" means. "Damage" is the opposite. "Tidy" attracts because both suggest putting something right, but a tidy room was never broken. "Conceal" fits the idea of hiding a flaw rather than fixing it, and "scold" only borrows the phrase "mend your ways" without meaning it.

"Peril" means serious exposure to harm, so "danger" matches it directly. "Safety" is the opposite condition. "Rescue" and "fear" belong to the same scene as peril without meaning it: one is the response to it, the other the feeling it causes. "Hardship" names difficulty already suffered, not the threat of harm ahead.

A "novice" is someone new to an activity, so "beginner" is the match. "Expert" reverses it. "Monk" tempts anyone recalling that a novice in a monastery is preparing to take vows, but a novice is precisely not yet a monk. "Volunteer" describes why someone joined, not how little experience they have, and "spectator" describes someone watching rather than starting out.

"Placid" describes something undisturbed and peaceful, so "calm" is the synonym. "Stormy" is its opposite. "Sluggish" adds slowness that placid does not require, and "agreeable" adds pleasantness of temper rather than stillness. "Shallow" is pulled in by the familiar phrase about a placid lake, but depth has nothing to do with the word.

To "quell" a riot or a rumor is to put a stop to it, which is what "suppress" means. "Provoke" is the reverse action. "Surrender" is what the quelled side does, not what the queller does. "Endure" means to bear something rather than to end it, and "complain" merely voices objection without stopping anything.

"Reticent" means disinclined to speak freely, so "reserved" fits. "Unwilling" is the trap: it defines a similar-sounding word about refusing to act, while reticence concerns holding back speech in particular. "Talkative" is the opposite. "Courteous" describes good manners, which a quiet person may or may not have, and "forgetful" explains silence by memory rather than by temperament.

A "meager" portion is far too small, and "scanty" carries that same sense of falling short. "Plentiful" is the opposite. "Keen" is the meaning of a near-twin word about eagerness, not about quantity. "Stingy" describes a person unwilling to give, whereas a meager meal may be all a generous host has. "Weary" borrows the bleak tone of the word without its meaning.

To "mollify" someone is to calm that person's anger, which is what "appease" means. "Enrage" is the opposite. "Pamper" indulges a person who need not be angry at all. "Clarify" is a plausible guess for anyone who hears a word ending in the same way and assumes it means making something plain, and "postpone" only delays the quarrel instead of soothing it.

"Prosaic" describes writing or living that is commonplace and unexciting, so "dull" is the match. "Poetic" is the contrast the word is built against. "Factual" tempts by way of prose and plain statement, but a report can be strictly factual and still vivid. "Profitable" is the meaning of a similar-looking word about thriving, and "brief" confuses plainness with shortness.

A "mercurial" temper shifts without warning, so "changeable" is the synonym. "Steady" is its opposite. "Poisonous" belongs to the metal that gave the word its name rather than to the word itself. "Forgiving" is the meaning of a look-alike word about mercy, and "boastful" supplies a different unpleasant trait entirely.

A "branch" is one part of a whole "tree," and a "chapter" is one part of a whole "novel." "tree is to branch" states the same relation backwards, whole before part. "forest is to shade" links a place to something it produces, not a part to its whole. "lumberjack is to axe" pairs a worker with a tool, and "root is to soil" pairs a thing with where it sits; both borrow the tree topic without repeating the part-to-whole link.

A "chef" works with a "knife," and a "gardener" works with a "trowel": worker followed by the tool of the trade. "wrench is to plumber" gives the tool first and so runs the relation backwards. "baker is to bread" names what the worker makes, not what the worker uses. "chef is to restaurant" names a workplace, and "recipe is to ingredient" is a whole and one of its listed parts.

"Cool" is a mild condition and "frigid" is its extreme form; "damp" is mild wetness and "saturated" is its extreme. "scorching is to warm" moves from extreme down to mild, the reverse of the stem. "winter is to snow" is a season and something it brings. "ice is to glacier" tempts because a glacier is larger, but it names a mass made of ice rather than a stronger degree of the same quality. "thirsty is to hungry" pairs two different appetites at equal strength.

A "drought" brings about a "famine," and "friction" brings about "heat": cause first, effect second. "flood is to rain" names the effect before its cause and so runs backwards. "desert is to sand" gives a place and what covers it. "farmer is to crop" is a worker and what the worker raises. "reservoir is to water" is a container and its contents; three of these stay near the stem's topic of dry land and hunger without repeating the causal link.

An "oboe" is one kind of "instrument," and an "opal" is one kind of "gem": broad category first, member second. "sonnet is to poem" puts the member first and the category second, reversing the stem. "oboe is to reed" moves from a whole to one of its parts. "orchestra is to conductor" pairs a group with the person leading it, and "flute is to melody" pairs a maker with what it produces.

A "broom" exists in order to "sweep," and a "shovel" exists in order to "dig": object followed by its function. "stir is to spoon" names the action before the object and so runs the relation backwards. "janitor is to hallway" gives a worker and a place. "mop is to bucket" names two objects often used together, neither being the purpose of the other. "dust is to allergy" is a cause and its effect.

"Ascend" and "descend" are opposites given in the order rise-then-fall, and "inflate" and "deflate" are opposites in that same order, swelling then shrinking. "retreat is to advance" is also a pair of opposites but runs fall-then-rise, the reverse of the stem's direction, so it does not match. "ladder is to rung" is a whole and one of its parts. "soar is to glide" names two kinds of flight that are not opposed at all. "staircase is to lobby" pairs an object with a place.

A "cartographer" produces a "map," and a "vintner" produces "wine": maker followed by the thing made. "sonata is to composer" names the product before its maker and so runs backwards. "surveyor is to theodolite" pairs a worker with an instrument rather than an output. "geographer is to terrain" names what a worker studies, which is found rather than made. "atlas is to map" is a whole and one of the pages it collects.

Being "deceitful" is the defining quality of a "charlatan," and being "stingy" is the defining quality of a "miser": person followed by the trait that makes the person that person. "generous is to philanthropist" gives the trait first and the person second, reversing the stem. "impostor is to costume" names a prop rather than a quality. "skeptic is to persuaded" names a state a skeptic resists. "sage is to elderly" is the closest trap, since sages are often old, but age is incidental while wisdom is what defines the word.

"Cargo" is stored in a ship's "hold," and "grain" is stored in a "silo": the thing first, the place that houses it second. "vault is to bullion" names the storage place before the goods and so runs the relation backwards. "ship is to captain" pairs a vessel with the person commanding it. "sailor is to voyage" pairs a person with an undertaking, not a location. "manifest is to shipment" pairs a written record with the goods it lists.

"Meager" and "scant" mean the same thing, so the answer must be another pair of near-synonyms: "hasty" and "hurried". "Generous" and "stingy" are opposites. "Starving" and "hungry" differ in intensity rather than being equivalent, and they run from the stronger word to the weaker one. A "meal" contains a "portion", a part-to-whole link stated backward. "Thrifty" and "wealthy" are merely related ideas about money, not equivalents.

A "murmur" is a faint version of what a "shout" is at full force, so the pair moves from mild to extreme; "drizzle" to "downpour" makes the same climb. "Gale" to "breeze" is the same scale run downward. "Whisper" and "secret" pair an act with what it may carry. "Chatter" is one kind of talk within a "conversation", not a weaker form of it. A "lecture" is delivered by a "lecturer", which links a product to a person.

An "orchard" is the place that yields "fruit", and a "mine" is the place that yields "ore". "Pear" to "orchard" states the same source-and-yield link backward. A "gardener" performs "pruning", which is a worker and a task. "Harvest" and "autumn" name an event and its season. A "loom" is the tool a "weaver" handles.

A "sextant" is the instrument a "navigator" works with, and a "trowel" is the instrument a "mason" works with. "Surveyor" to "theodolite" puts the worker first and the tool second, reversing the order. A "compass" produces a "bearing", which pairs a tool with its reading rather than its user. A "chart" is consulted during a "voyage", linking an object to an occasion. An "anvil" is used to shape a "horseshoe", pairing a tool with the thing it makes.

A "petal" is one component of a "blossom", just as a "rung" is one component of a "ladder". "Orchestra" to "violin" gives the whole before the part, reversing the order. A "blossom" gives off a "fragrance", a thing and a quality it emits. A "garden" is tended by a "gardener", a place and a person. "Bud" and "bloom" are two stages of one growth, not a piece and the thing it belongs to.

"Neglect" brings about "decay", and "friction" brings about "heat", so each pair moves from a cause to what it produces. "Erosion" to "rainfall" names the result before the force that drives it, reversing the order. "Rot" and "timber" pair a condition with the material it afflicts. "Repair" and "restoration" are close in meaning rather than one producing the other. A "custodian" performs "upkeep", linking a person to a duty.

A "pen" exists in order to "write", and a "broom" exists in order to "sweep". "Erase" to "eraser" states the same purpose link backward, naming the action first. "Ink" is held in a "cartridge", a substance and its container. A "typist" operates a "keyboard", a person and a device. "Chalk" is applied to a "blackboard", a tool and the surface it marks rather than the job it performs.

To "squander" is the reverse of to "conserve", and to "conceal" is the reverse of to "reveal". "Hoard" and "accumulate" mean nearly the same thing. To "spend" is how one makes a "purchase", a means and its result. "Chilly" and "frigid" sit on one scale of cold, differing only in strength. "Frugal" and "allowance" pair a trait with money it might govern.

An "iguana" is one kind of "reptile", and a "sonnet" is one kind of "poem", each pair naming the class and then a member of it. "Python" to "reptile" names the member first, reversing the order. A "lizard" is covered in "scales", a creature and a feature it bears. "Amphibian" and "reptile" are two classes side by side, neither contained in the other. "Mammal" and "warm-blooded" pair a class with a trait, not with an example.

"Fervor" is the quality that defines a "zealot", and "solitude" is the quality that defines a "recluse". "Generosity" to "philanthropist" names the trait before the person, reversing the order. A "fanatic" attaches himself to a "cause", pairing a person with an object of loyalty. A "devotee" visits a "shrine", pairing a person with a place. "Apathy" and "indifference" are two names for one thing rather than a person and a defining trait.

A summit is the highest point of a mountain, so "peak" matches it exactly. "Base" names the bottom instead. "Slope" belongs to the same mountain vocabulary but is not the top. "Summary" merely looks and sounds like the stem. "Delegate" belongs to the other sense of summit, a meeting of leaders, but a delegate is a person at such a meeting, not the meeting itself.

Timid means easily frightened and hesitant around others, which is what "shy" means. "Bold" is the direct opposite. "Tiny" resembles the stem in sound and gets confused with it, but it describes size, not nerve. "Obedient" describes doing as told, which a bold person can also do. "Clumsy" describes awkward movement rather than fearfulness.

Something tacit is understood or agreed to without ever being put into words, so "unspoken" fits. "Explicit" names the opposite, something stated outright. "Tactful" only shares an opening sound and means considerate in speech. "Unanimous" is attracted by the common phrase about agreement but describes how many agree, not whether it was said. "Reluctant" describes unwillingness, which a tacit agreement need not involve.

To squander money, time, or a chance is to spend it uselessly, which is exactly what "waste" means. "Hoard" is the opposite behavior, holding everything back. "Squabble" merely begins like the stem and means to quarrel. "Inherit" belongs to the same money vocabulary but names getting wealth, not throwing it away. "Misplace" tempts because both end in loss, but misplacing is accidental and temporary while squandering is the act of using something up badly.

When enthusiasm or the moon wanes it grows steadily smaller, which is what "dwindle" means. "Swell" names the opposite motion. "Wander" resembles the stem in spelling and sound only. "Pale" is attracted by the related-looking word describing a sickly color, but losing color is not the same as decreasing. "Linger" describes lasting longer than expected, nearly the reverse of fading away.

A zealous supporter is filled with intense eagerness for a cause, which "fervent" captures. "Indifferent" names the opposite state, caring not at all. "Jealous" rhymes with the stem and is constantly confused with it, but it means resentful of what another has. "Generous" describes giving freely, which enthusiasm does not require. "Cautious" describes holding back, the temper opposite of eager.

To temper a judgment or a demand is to soften it and keep it within limits, which is what "moderate" means. "Intensify" names the opposite effect. "Harden" comes from the metalworking use of the word, but tempering metal reheats it to reduce brittleness rather than to make it harder. "Provoke" belongs with the familiar noun sense about anger without meaning the stem. "Tempest" merely shares an opening and names a storm.

A specious argument looks sound at first but is false underneath, so "misleading" fits. "Genuine" is its opposite. "Particular" is pulled in by the similar-looking root behind words like specify. "Rare" comes from confusing the stem with special. "Courteous" tempts because a specious claim is smooth and pleasing on the surface, but politeness is a manner, not a falsehood.

Truculent describes someone aggressively defiant and spoiling for a fight, which "belligerent" names. "Amiable" is the opposite disposition. "Truthful" is drawn from the false resemblance to truth at the start of the stem. "Succulent" echoes the ending only and describes juicy food. "Exhausted" tempts because a truculent person is often described as sullen and worn out, but weariness is not hostility.
